title: Bill Phillips, his first band, and teacher Milford Piron
summary: Albert recalls playing in Bill Phillips's band, his teacher stopping lessons, and his two years of studying with Milford Piron; Phillips's later life and friendship are described.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You said that Dick Allen had asked you to get a few questions for me?
Yeah. You said that uh... A few questions and he wanted me to tell you a few things. That's mighty fine. Or maybe you could tell me about Bill Phillips.
Bill Phillips, my drummer? Yeah. Oh man, sure, I'd be happy to. But before I do that, this is my son here that was serving in the Korean War.

This is Kenneth. Is he here? He's here, but he's over at his house with his wife. I believe Bill met him. Yes. He came in just as Bill was completing the interview. And he is 31 years old now. Did he play anything? No, he never did want music. Now we'll get back to Bill Phillips. That is the first band that I actually played with and he was the cause that my professor stopped teaching me. Bill Phillips came to get me to play with his band and my professor didn't think that I should play in a band but he had never mentioned it to me. So when I came to take my lessons one night he told me, he says, well I don't think you need any more lessons now. You're a finished musician. I heard you playing in a band. Well from that I went on out and of course I had a very, very good knowledge of music because I had studied under Milford Piron for almost two years without an instrument just reading music out of a book and beating the time with my hand and reading the music as it was and singing it. For how long you did that? Almost two years. No kidding. That's right. That's why Paul, I'm not ashamed to say it, I don't know whether you noticed or not, but I'm not afraid to put anybody's music in front of me and read it at sight. I don't say that I'll play it perfect but I will play it.
Was Milford Piron akin to AJ?
That's AJ's older brother. I see. Piron is cousin, Armand Piron is cousin to me through marriage.
Well Dick said to tell you that Bill Phillips is a bass drummer now with the Young Tuxedo Brass Band.
And he has a vegetable truck and he's doing very well.

Good. I visit Bill every time I go to New Orleans and Ida always fixes what I used to like to eat over there and every time I go there I say, Don, I've got your dish cooked for you. What's that? Dumbo and rice. Yeah. That's right. And I go over there and Bill just stacks up my automobile with all the fruit. Oh yeah? And I can't pay him for it. I try to pay, he says no you don't pay. Probably hit you with his bass drum beater. And he also played my wedding. See when I left New Orleans I was a kid but I was engaged to my wife and when they announced the wedding, well Bill got all of the musicians to, I didn't even know they were going to do that, and they gathered in the house at 1677 North Mero Street that night at eight o'clock. And they all played and they weren't satisfied until I sat in the band to play something with them. So you know on my first wedding night I didn't want to play too much. No. But I did play a little. I think that was kind. That's right. But Bill Phillips always been a very, very great friend of mine. I've always admired Bill Phillips because he's been a gentleman ever since I've known him.
